claims.text: The initial Fe-Co-Ni-Ti high-entropy alloy is a single-phase fcc matrix.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti has suppressed orbital moments and low coercivity.
The low coercivity of the single-phase alloy results from weak magnetic anisotropy and insufficient domain-wall pinning.
Annealing at 973–1273 K can precipitate an Al-rich or Ti-rich B2 phase within fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti.
A 5–10 vol% B2 precipitate fraction can be introduced while retaining continuity of the fcc matrix.
The proposed Al-rich or Ti-rich B2 precipitates will be ferromagnetic.
The B2 precipitates will form coherent or semi-coherent interfaces with the fcc matrix.
The fcc/B2 interfaces will act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Strain coupling at fcc/B2 interfaces will enhance local magnetic anisotropy.
The B2 phase will provide a high-moment ferromagnetic component with magnetic anisotropy distinct from that of the fcc matrix.
Interfacial exchange-spring or pinning effects will impede domain-wall motion and raise room-temperature coercivity above 100 Oe.
The dual-phase alloy will retain a Curie temperature above 300 K and could approach or exceed 390 K if B2 dominates the magnetic ordering.
The dual-phase alloy will have saturation magnetization comparable to or slightly lower than the single-phase alloy.
The single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti baseline has coercivity below 20 Oe.
The single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti baseline has a Curie temperature above 300 K.
In Cr-containing Fe-Co-Ni-related alloys, high Cr content can produce antiferromagnetic alignment or paramagnetism and reduce the net magnetic moment.
Excess Ti can make the proposed secondary phase antiferromagnetic or paramagnetic.
The secondary-phase fraction must be large enough to create a sufficiently connected population of pinning sites.
An excessive secondary-phase fraction would disrupt fcc-matrix continuity and compromise the high Curie temperature.
Rapid quenching can suppress B2 precipitation at fixed bulk composition and therefore provide a valid single-phase control.
